what: AeroVironment makes drones and military systems for the US and allied militaries: small surveillance drones such as Puma, Switchblade loitering munitions, and, since buying BlueHalo in 2025, space, electronic warfare and counter-drone systems.
customers: The US Army, Marine Corps and Special Operations Command, and allied militaries including Ukraine’s.
money: Space systems, electronic warfare and counter-drone products.
moat: Proven combat systems used in Ukraine and a long relationship with US forces, in categories the Pentagon is prioritising.
risks: The BlueHalo purchase brought losses from amortisation and integration: $203M over the last twelve months.
Revenue depends on government budgets and contract timing.
Competition from venture-backed defence start-ups such as Anduril.
Free cash flow is near zero.
opportunities: Revenue more than doubled to about $2.0B with BlueHalo.
Drones and counter-drone systems are top Pentagon priorities.
Twenty-four analysts average a target above $200, more than double the price.
watch: Switchblade orders, counter-drone contracts and BlueHalo integration.
view: AeroVironment sits in the defence categories growing fastest: drones, loitering munitions and counter-drone systems, all proven in Ukraine. Buying BlueHalo more than doubled revenue to about $2 billion, though the deal costs have pushed it into a GAAP loss.

The share price has fallen sharply, and the analysts’ average target is now more than double. The market worries about integration, contract timing and competition from start-ups. At about 26 times forward earnings, the valuation is no longer stretched for a company with this exposure.

This turns on contract wins and the BlueHalo integration. I think the strategic position is strong, but defence contractors are lumpy and integration takes time, so it looks attractive mainly for patient investors.
bull: Drone and counter-drone demand grows for years and BlueHalo integration pays off.
bear: Contracts slip, integration costs linger and start-ups take share.
